documents.title: Alligator vs Caiman
documents.description: Alligators and caimans are the two subfamilies of Alligatoridae, separated by continent: alligators in North America and China, caimans in Central and South America.

documents.title: Alpaca vs Goat
documents.description: An alpaca is a hornless camelid grazer that feeds across level pasture; a goat is a horned bovid browser that climbs and strips leaves, shoots and bark.

documents.title: Alpaca vs Llama
documents.description: A llama is the larger camelid with long curved ears and a bare-ish long face; an alpaca is smaller, with short straight ears and dense fleece covering its face.

documents.title: Alpaca vs Sheep
documents.description: An alpaca is a long-necked camelid on padded two-toed feet with a three-chambered stomach; a sheep is a bovid on cloven hooves with a four-chambered ruminant stomach.

documents.title: Anaconda vs Reticulated Python
documents.description: The reticulated python is the longest snake and the green anaconda the heaviest, and the difference in build reflects an aquatic ambusher against a terrestrial and arboreal one.

documents.title: Andean Condor vs California Condor
documents.description: White on the upper wing plus a fleshy crown comb marks an adult male Andean condor, while white on the underwing and no comb at all marks a California condor.

documents.title: Angelfish vs Clownfish
documents.description: Clownfish are anemone-dwelling damselfishes with a single identity, whereas angelfish is a name shared by an Amazonian cichlid and an unrelated marine reef family.

documents.title: Anglerfish vs Frogfish
documents.description: Frogfish are shallow-water anglerfish with an unlit fleshy lure, whereas the deep-sea ceratioids everyone pictures light their lure with symbiotic bacteria.

documents.title: Ant vs Leafcutter Ant
documents.description: Ant names the whole family Formicidae; leafcutter ant names the American genera Atta and Acromyrmex, which cut vegetation to feed a cultivated fungus rather than eating the leaves themselves.

documents.title: Ant vs Termite
documents.description: Ants are hymenopterans with a pinched waist and elbowed antennae; termites are social cockroaches with a straight body and beaded antennae, and the two lineages evolved sociality independently.

documents.title: Armadillo vs Pangolin
documents.description: Armadillo armour is bone formed inside the skin, while pangolin armour is overlapping keratin scales, and the two belong to separate mammal orders on separate continents.

documents.title: Axolotl vs Tiger Salamander
documents.description: The axolotl retains its larval form and gills for life while reaching sexual maturity, whereas the tiger salamander metamorphoses into a terrestrial adult.

documents.title: Baboon vs Mandrill
documents.description: A mandrill is a rainforest monkey in the genus Mandrillus with a stub tail and a colour-ridged male face; baboons are open-country monkeys in Papio with long kinked tails and plain fur-covered…

documents.title: Barn Owl vs Snowy Owl
documents.description: The barn owl is a pale, dark-eyed, heart-faced bird of the family Tytonidae, while the snowy owl is a large yellow-eyed tundra owl in Strigidae — they are relatives only at the level of the owl order.

documents.title: Barnacle vs Limpet
documents.description: A barnacle's cone is a ring of separate plates with a lid it opens to feed, while a limpet's cone is one solid piece over a snail that grazes and then returns to its resting scar.

documents.title: Beaver vs Capybara
documents.description: A beaver has a flat scaly paddle tail and builds dams and lodges from felled wood; a capybara has no visible tail and grazes wetland grass in South American herds without building anything.

documents.title: Bee vs Bumblebee
documents.description: Bee names the whole clade Anthophila with over 20,000 species; bumblebee names one genus inside it, Bombus, defined by dense fur, annual colonies and buzz pollination.

documents.title: Bee vs Butterfly
documents.description: Bees collect pollen deliberately to provision their young and are built to carry it; butterflies seek only nectar and move pollen incidentally.

documents.title: Bee vs Hoverfly
documents.description: A hoverfly is a two-winged fly that mimics bee colouration for protection and cannot sting; a bee is a four-winged hymenopteran that can.

documents.title: Bee vs Wasp
documents.description: Bees feed their larvae on pollen and nectar and are built to carry pollen; wasps feed their larvae on animal prey and are built to catch it.

documents.title: Betta Fish vs Angelfish
documents.description: The betta is an air-breathing anabantoid whose males tend bubble nests; the freshwater angelfish is a deep-bodied cichlid whose pairs guard eggs laid on a vertical surface.

documents.title: Betta Fish vs Guppy
documents.description: Bettas are air-breathing, territorial fish that cannot be housed with other males; guppies are social livebearers that reproduce prolifically.

documents.title: Bison vs African Buffalo
documents.description: A bison has a shoulder hump, beard and side-set horns and lives in North America and Europe; an African buffalo has no hump and heavy fused horns, and the two are not close relatives.

documents.title: Brown Bear vs American Black Bear
documents.description: A shoulder hump, dished face and long straight fore claws mark a brown bear; a humpless back with the rump highest, a straight profile and short hooked claws mark an American black bear.

documents.title: Brown Bear vs Asian Black Bear
documents.description: The Asian black bear is a smaller, canopy-feeding forest bear with a pale chest crescent and large ears; the brown bear is a bulkier, humped, ground-foraging omnivore with no chest mark.

documents.title: Brown Bear vs Polar Bear
documents.description: The brown bear is a humped, long-clawed omnivore that dens through winter; the polar bear is a white, long-skulled seal hunter tied to Arctic sea ice and active all year.

documents.title: Bullfrog vs Cane Toad
documents.description: The bullfrog is an aquatic predator that eats and out-competes native species, while the cane toad is a terrestrial toad whose skin toxin poisons the predators that attack it.

documents.title: Butterfly vs Moth
documents.description: Butterflies form a clade nested within Lepidoptera, so all butterflies are technically moths in the broad sense; the everyday cues that separate them are antenna shape, activity period and pupal form.

documents.title: Caecilian vs Snake
documents.description: A caecilian is an amphibian with ringed, permeable skin and a sensory tentacle; a snake is a reptile with dry scales and a forked tongue.

documents.title: Camel vs Dromedary
documents.description: Camel is the genus-level name covering three living species; dromedary is one of them, the one-humped camel of Arabia and North Africa.

documents.title: Camel vs Llama
documents.description: Camels are the humped Old World camelids of African and Asian drylands, while the llama is a humpless Andean camelid domesticated from the guanaco.

documents.title: Caracal vs Serval
documents.description: A serval is a tall, long-legged spotted cat with huge round untufted ears; a caracal is a stockier plain tawny cat with narrow black-backed ears carrying long tufts.

documents.title: Cat vs Ferret
documents.description: A cat is a feliform ambush predator with retractile claws and a comparatively long life; a ferret is a caniform tunnel specialist whose gut empties within hours and whose typical lifespan is around…

documents.title: Cat vs Rabbit
documents.description: A cat is an obligate carnivore built to detect and catch small mammals, while a rabbit is a hindgut-fermenting prey herbivore built to detect and outrun them, and it re-ingests its own soft faeces to…

documents.title: Centipede vs Millipede
documents.description: Centipedes have one pair of legs per segment and are venomous predators; millipedes have two pairs per segment and are harmless decomposers.

documents.title: Chameleon vs Octopus
documents.description: A chameleon changes colour by tuning structural crystal lattices, chiefly for signalling; an octopus does it with nerve-controlled pigment sacs, chiefly for camouflage, and far faster.

documents.title: Chicken vs Duck
documents.description: Webbed feet, a flat straining bill and oiled waterproof down mark the duck; clawed scratching feet, a pointed beak and a comb with wattles mark the chicken.

documents.title: Chicken vs Goose
documents.description: A goose crops grass with a serrated bill on a long neck and defends a family with loud calls and display; a chicken scratches litter, pecks individual items and roosts off the ground.

documents.title: Chicken vs Pigeon
documents.description: A chicken hatches self-feeding chicks and stays close to the ground; a pigeon hatches helpless squabs raised on crop milk and flies strongly over long distances.

documents.title: Chicken vs Wild Turkey
documents.description: The chicken is a domesticated junglefowl descendant with a comb and wattles; the wild turkey is a much larger free-living North American bird with a bare caruncled head, a snood and a tree-roosting…

documents.title: Chimpanzee vs Orangutan
documents.description: Chimpanzees are black-haired, ground-capable and intensely social African apes; orangutans are red-haired, canopy-living and largely solitary Asian apes whose dominant males grow cheek flanges.

documents.title: Chinchilla vs Guinea Pig
documents.description: Both are South American caviomorphs, but the chinchilla is a lightly built high-altitude leaper with an extreme coat, while the guinea pig is a heavier grazer that must take vitamin C from its food.

documents.title: Chinchilla vs Hamster
documents.description: A chinchilla is a long-lived, colony-forming Andean herbivore; a hamster is a short-lived solitary steppe omnivore that hoards food in cheek pouches.

documents.title: Cicada vs Grasshopper
documents.description: A cicada is a hemipteran that sucks xylem sap through a beak and sings with abdominal tymbals; a grasshopper is an orthopteran that chews leaves and stridulates with its hind legs.

documents.title: Clam vs Oyster
documents.description: Clams burrow into sediment using a muscular foot, while oysters cement one shell permanently to a hard surface and accumulate into reefs.

documents.title: Clouded Leopard vs Leopard
documents.description: A clouded leopard is a much smaller cat in the genus Neofelis with large cloud-shaped blotches, while the leopard is a Panthera big cat covered in small tight rosettes.

documents.title: Cobra vs Viper
documents.description: Cobras are elapids with short fixed fangs and slender bodies; vipers are a separate family with long hinged fangs that fold away when not in use.

documents.title: Coconut Crab vs Hermit Crab
documents.description: Adult coconut crabs discard the borrowed shell and harden their own abdomen, while hermit crabs keep moving into progressively larger gastropod shells for life.

documents.title: Coral Snake vs King Cobra
documents.description: Both are elapids, but the coral snake is a small banded burrower relying on warning colouration, while the king cobra is the longest venomous snake, a snake specialist that builds a nest.

documents.title: Coral vs Sea Anemone
documents.description: A stony coral secretes an aragonite skeleton and grows as a colony, while a sea anemone is one skeleton-free polyp that can release its grip and relocate.

documents.title: Cougar vs Leopard
documents.description: The cougar fills the adaptable solitary mid-large cat role in the Americas without spots, while the leopard fills the same role across Africa and Asia with rosettes and a stronger tree-caching habit.

documents.title: Cow vs African Buffalo
documents.description: Cattle were domesticated from the aurochs, while the African buffalo is a separate genus whose temperament and herd defence prevented domestication.

documents.title: Cow vs Goat
documents.description: Cattle are large grazers that sweep the tongue around grass at ground level; goats are small browsers that use a mobile lip to strip leaves, shoots and bark, often while climbing.

documents.title: Cow vs Horse
documents.description: A cow is a cloven-hoofed ruminant that ferments forage in a four-chambered stomach and chews the cud; a horse is a single-toed hindgut fermenter that processes fibre behind the stomach and grazes…

documents.title: Cow vs Sheep
documents.description: Cattle tear tall grass by sweeping it up with the tongue, while sheep bite it close to the ground with a cleft upper lip, so the two leave completely different swards behind them.

documents.title: Coyote vs Fox
documents.description: A coyote is a substantially larger, longer-legged canid with round pupils; a fox is smaller and slighter with vertical pupils and a proportionally longer tail.

documents.title: Crab vs Lobster
documents.description: A crab has a reduced abdomen folded under a broad shell and walks sideways; a lobster keeps a long muscular abdomen extended for rapid backwards escape.

documents.title: Crocodile vs Caiman
documents.description: A caiman is an alligatorid restricted to the Americas with a hidden fourth lower tooth and bony belly armour; a crocodile is a crocodylid found across several continents with that tooth exposed when…

documents.title: Damselfly vs Antlion
documents.description: An antlion carries short clubbed antennae, flies mainly after dusk and grows up buried in dry ground; a damselfly has bristle antennae, flies by day and grows up underwater.

documents.title: Damselfly vs Butterfly
documents.description: A butterfly has scale-covered wings and a coiled drinking tube; a damselfly has bare membranous wings and mandibles for eating captured insects.

documents.title: Damselfly vs Cicada
documents.description: Both grow gradually and hide their long immature stage, but a damselfly nymph is an aquatic predator while a cicada nymph is a subterranean sap-feeder.

documents.title: Damselfly vs Dragonfly
documents.description: A damselfly folds its matched narrow wings along the body and has widely separated eyes; a dragonfly spreads broader-based hindwings flat and usually has eyes touching over the head.

documents.title: Damselfly vs Hoverfly
documents.description: A damselfly hovers on four independently steered wings, while a hoverfly hovers on one pair beating far faster and stabilised by halteres, the reduced hindwings unique to flies.

documents.title: Damselfly vs Lacewing
documents.description: A damselfly is an odonate with bristle-short antennae and aquatic nymphs; a lacewing is a neuropteran with long thread antennae and terrestrial larvae that pupate.

documents.title: Damselfly vs Mayfly
documents.description: A mayfly trails long tail filaments, holds its wings upright and cannot feed as an adult; a damselfly has no filaments, four matched wings folded along the body, and hunts on the wing.

documents.title: Dingo vs Wolf
documents.description: The dingo descends from early domestic dogs that returned to independent living, while the wolf is a wild species that was never domesticated; the dingo is also far smaller.

documents.title: Dog vs Cat
documents.description: Cats are obligate carnivores descended from a solitary ancestor; dogs are dietary generalists descended from cooperative pack hunters, and that shapes almost everything else.

documents.title: Dog vs Ferret
documents.description: A dog is a canid bred for cooperative work in the open and reads human cues unusually well; a ferret is a mustelid bred to work alone in burrows and keeps a solitary, high-sleep, tunnel-shaped…

documents.title: Dog vs Rabbit
documents.description: A dog is a cursorial canid predator that signals its state loudly and openly, while a rabbit is a burrowing lagomorph prey animal that signals distress by going quiet and still, so the two must be…

documents.title: Dolphin vs Orca
documents.description: The orca is the largest dolphin, distinguished by size, a very tall dorsal fin, and populations that form culturally distinct ecotypes with separate diets and dialects.

documents.title: Dolphin vs Porpoise
documents.description: Dolphins have conical teeth, usually a beak and a hooked dorsal fin; porpoises have spade-shaped teeth, a blunt face and a low triangular fin.

documents.title: Dolphin vs Shark
documents.description: A dolphin is an air-breathing mammal whose ancestors returned to the sea from land; a shark is a cartilaginous fish whose lineage never left it, and their resemblance is convergent rather than…

documents.title: Dolphin vs Whale
documents.description: Dolphins are a family within the toothed whales, so every dolphin is a whale; the meaningful cetacean division is between toothed and baleen species.

documents.title: Donkey vs Horse
documents.description: A donkey is a desert-derived equid with long ears, an upright mane, a tufted tail and 62 chromosomes; a horse is a grassland equid with a falling mane, a full tail and 64.

documents.title: Donkey vs Zebra
documents.description: A donkey is one domesticated species descended from the African wild ass; zebra is a name covering three African species that were never domesticated, all of them striped.

documents.title: Dromedary vs Llama
documents.description: The dromedary is a humped Old World camel of hot desert; the llama is a humpless New World camelid of the cold high Andes, and the two branches diverged long ago.

documents.title: Duck vs Goose
documents.description: Geese are larger, longer-necked land grazers with long-term pair bonds and shared parental care; ducks are smaller water feeders where the female usually raises the brood alone.

documents.title: Duck vs Swan
documents.description: A swan is a very large, long-necked waterfowl that raises grey cygnets with a long-term mate; a duck is a compact, short-necked waterfowl with mostly seasonal pairings.

documents.title: Eagle vs Hawk
documents.description: Both sit within the family Accipitridae, and the difference is one of size, bill and foot power rather than a taxonomic split, with eagle reserved for the largest and most powerfully built members.

documents.title: Eagle vs Vulture
documents.description: Eagles have powerful gripping feet for killing live prey, while vultures have weak walking feet and bare heads suited to scavenging carcasses.

documents.title: Earthworm vs Velvet Worm
documents.description: An earthworm is a legless segmented annelid that eats soil, while a velvet worm is a clawed-legged onychophoran predator with a dry velvety cuticle and antennae.

documents.title: Eel vs Electric Eel
documents.description: The electric eel is a South American knifefish related to catfish, not an eel; true eels are a separate order that migrates to sea to spawn.

documents.title: Eel vs Moray Eel
documents.description: Eel names the order Anguilliformes; morays are one family within it, set apart by round gill pores, absent pectoral fins and pharyngeal jaws in the throat.

documents.title: Emu vs Cassowary
documents.description: A cassowary has a keratin casque, glossy black plumage and rainforest habits; an emu is casque-free, grey-brown and shaggy, and lives in open country.

documents.title: Ferret vs Guinea Pig
documents.description: A ferret is an elongated mustelid carnivore built to enter burrows; a guinea pig is a barrel-bodied grazing rodent that must obtain vitamin C from its food.

documents.title: Ferret vs Hamster
documents.description: A ferret is a carnivorous mustelid built around meat, movement and supervised out-of-cage time; a hamster is a solitary seed-hoarding rodent living on a nocturnal schedule.

documents.title: Ferret vs Rabbit
documents.description: A ferret is a domesticated polecat whose obligate-carnivore gut empties within hours; a rabbit is a lagomorph fermenter whose gut must never stop receiving fibre.

documents.title: Ferret vs Weasel
documents.description: The ferret is a domesticated descendant of the European polecat, while the weasel is a separate wild species that has never been domesticated.

documents.title: Flamingo vs Stork
documents.description: A flamingo filters tiny food from water with a kinked bill held upside down; a stork grasps whole prey with a long straight bill.

documents.title: Frog vs Toad
documents.description: All toads are frogs; toad picks out drier-skinned, shorter-legged, more terrestrial anurans, with the name most strictly applied to the true toads of the family Bufonidae.

documents.title: Garter Snake vs Grass Snake
documents.description: A garter snake wears pale lengthwise stripes and gives birth to live young; a grass snake wears a pale collar behind the head and lays eggs.

documents.title: Gecko vs Skink
documents.description: Geckos have granular skin, mostly lidless eyes and often adhesive toe pads for climbing; skinks have smooth overlapping scales, movable eyelids and a low-slung ground-dwelling build.

documents.title: Gecko vs Tokay Gecko
documents.description: Gecko is an infraorder-level label for a huge worldwide radiation of lizards; the tokay is one large, vividly spotted Asian species inside it.

documents.title: Gerbil vs Guinea Pig
documents.description: A gerbil is an arid-country tunneller whose defining need is deep substrate to dig in; a guinea pig is a surface-grazing Andean rodent whose defining needs are companionship and continuous fibre.

documents.title: Gerbil vs Mouse
documents.description: A gerbil has a fully furred, tuft-tipped tail and dry-country water physiology; a house mouse has a scaly near-naked tail and thrives commensally wherever people store food.

documents.title: Gharial vs Crocodile
documents.description: A gharial's snout is a narrow fish-catching instrument and it belongs to a separate family; a crocodile's broader snout handles a wide range of prey across several continents.

documents.title: Giant Anteater vs Aardvark
documents.description: The giant anteater is a toothless South American xenarthran with a plume tail that walks on its knuckles; the aardvark is an African burrower in an order of its own with tall ears and rootless…

documents.title: Giraffe vs Okapi
documents.description: The okapi is the giraffe's only living relative: a short-necked forest browser striped across the hindquarters, set against the tall, blotched, open-country member of the same two-branch family.

documents.title: Glass Frog vs Red-Eyed Tree Frog
documents.description: A glass frog conceals itself by being partly see-through against a leaf, while a red-eyed tree frog conceals bright colours and then reveals them abruptly.

documents.title: Goat vs Sheep
documents.description: Goats are exploratory browsers that hold their tails up; sheep are grass-grazing flockers that hold their tails down.

documents.title: Goldfish vs Betta Fish
documents.description: A goldfish is a large-growing coldwater carp relative with a heavy waste output, while a betta is a small tropical labyrinth fish that breathes atmospheric air and cannot be held at goldfish…

documents.title: Goldfish vs Guppy
documents.description: A goldfish is a large coldwater cyprinid that scatters eggs and abandons them, while a guppy is a small tropical poeciliid whose females carry young internally and give birth to free-swimming fry.

documents.title: Goldfish vs Koi
documents.description: Koi have barbels at the mouth and grow far larger than goldfish, and the two descend from different wild carp ancestors.

documents.title: Gorilla vs Chimpanzee
documents.description: Gorillas are far heavier, mainly plant-eating and live in stable silverback-led groups, while chimpanzees are smaller, hunt and use tools routinely, and live in fluid fission-fusion communities.

documents.title: Gorilla vs Orangutan
documents.description: The gorilla is a terrestrial African ape built around bulk plant feeding and permanent group life; the orangutan is an arboreal Asian ape built around slow canopy travel and a semi-solitary range.

documents.title: Grasshopper vs Cricket
documents.description: Grasshoppers are short-horned Caelifera that stridulate leg against wing and hear through the abdomen; crickets are long-horned Ensifera that rub wing against wing and hear through the front tibiae.

documents.title: Great White Shark vs Hammerhead Shark
documents.description: The great white is one warm-muscled mackerel shark with a conical snout; hammerheads are a whole family of ground sharks built around a laterally expanded head.

documents.title: Green Sea Turtle vs Leatherback
documents.description: The leatherback has a leathery ridged carapace and a jellyfish diet with exceptional diving ability; the green sea turtle has a hard scuted shell and grazes seagrass in shallow coastal water.

documents.title: Guinea Pig vs Hamster
documents.description: Guinea pigs are social daytime herbivores with a dietary vitamin C requirement; hamsters are solitary nocturnal omnivores that hoard food.

documents.title: Guppy vs Tetra
documents.description: Guppies give birth to free-swimming young and show strong male-female difference; tetras scatter eggs, abandon them, and usually show little difference between the sexes.

documents.title: Hamster vs Gerbil
documents.description: A hamster is a stub-tailed, pouch-cheeked cricetid that usually lives alone; a Mongolian gerbil is a long furred-tailed, long-legged murid from arid Asia that lives in a family group.

documents.title: Hamster vs Mouse
documents.description: A hamster is a stocky, stub-tailed hoarder with cheek pouches and a burrowing life; a house mouse is a slim, long-tailed climber that has spread worldwide by living commensally with people.

documents.title: Hedgehog vs Porcupine
documents.description: A hedgehog is a small insectivore with short spines that never detach and a curl-into-a-ball defence; a porcupine is a large herbivorous rodent with long quills that release on contact.

documents.title: Hellbender vs Asian Giant Salamander
documents.description: The hellbender is the smaller American branch of the giant salamander family and retains open gill slits, while Asian Andrias species grow far larger and lose them.

documents.title: Hermit Crab vs Crab
documents.description: A hermit crab has a soft coiled abdomen that must be housed in a borrowed gastropod shell, while a true crab has a hardened symmetrical abdomen folded flat beneath its own carapace.

documents.title: Heron vs Sandhill Crane
documents.description: A sandhill crane extends its neck in flight, wears a feathered bustle over the tail and bugles; a heron folds its neck, carries fine plumes and croaks.

documents.title: Heron vs Stork
documents.description: A heron retracts its neck into an S in flight; a stork keeps it fully extended, and the rule holds right across both families.

documents.title: Horse vs Llama
documents.description: A horse is a single-toed equid domesticated on the Eurasian steppe and built to carry a rider; a llama is a two-toed Andean camelid used to carry loads rather than people.

documents.title: Horse vs Zebra
documents.description: Horses and zebras are close equid relatives, but zebra temperament and social structure lack the traits domestication requires, so only the horse was domesticated.

documents.title: Horseshoe Crab vs Crab
documents.description: A horseshoe crab is a chelicerate with book gills, chelicerae and no antennae, so its nearest relatives are arachnids, while a true crab is a decapod crustacean with antennae, mandibles and chamber…

documents.title: Hummingbird vs Sunbird
documents.description: Hummingbirds are American swift relatives built for sustained hovering; sunbirds are Old World songbirds that mostly perch to reach the same nectar.

documents.title: Hyena vs Aardwolf
documents.description: Both are hyaenids, but the aardwolf is a small insect specialist with reduced peg-like cheek teeth, while the other hyenas are meat and carrion feeders with robust bone-processing dentition.

documents.title: Iguana vs Chameleon
documents.description: A chameleon is a specialised arboreal hunter with independently moving eyes, a projectile tongue and grasping feet; an iguana is a larger, largely herbivorous lizard with conventional lizard anatomy.

documents.title: Jaguar vs Cougar
documents.description: A jaguar is a rosette-patterned, heavy-headed Panthera cat; a cougar is a plain tawny, small-headed Puma with a very long tail.

documents.title: Jellyfish vs Comb Jelly
documents.description: A jellyfish is a cnidarian that pulses a bell and stings with cnidocytes; a comb jelly is a ctenophore that rows on eight cilia rows and traps prey with sticky cells.

documents.title: Jellyfish vs Squid
documents.description: A jellyfish is a radially symmetrical cnidarian with a nerve net and stinging cells; a squid is a bilaterally symmetrical mollusc with a large brain, image-forming eyes and a beak.

documents.title: Kangaroo vs Wallaby
documents.description: Kangaroo and wallaby are both macropods; kangaroo names the four largest grazing species while wallaby is an informal size label covering many smaller species across several genera.

documents.title: Koala vs Wombat
documents.description: A koala is an arboreal eucalyptus specialist that grips branches; a wombat is a barrel-shaped burrower that grazes at ground level and digs its own tunnels.

documents.title: Koi vs Carp
documents.description: Koi are a domesticated ornamental form selected out of carp stock; carp is the wider common name for the wild and farmed cyprinids that form is descended from.

documents.title: Komodo Dragon vs Monitor Lizard
documents.description: Monitor lizard means the whole genus Varanus, while Komodo dragon is one species inside it, Varanus komodoensis, the largest living lizard and one restricted to a few Indonesian islands.

documents.title: Krill vs Shrimp
documents.description: Krill wear their gills on the outside of the carapace and filter plankton in open water; shrimp hide their gills in a chamber under the carapace and occupy far more habitats, including fresh water.

documents.title: Ladybug vs Stag Beetle
documents.description: A ladybug is a small domed aphid predator that matures in weeks; a stag beetle is a large deadwood grub that spends years underground before a brief winged adult stage.

documents.title: Lynx vs Bobcat
documents.description: The lynx is a deep-snow specialist with huge snowshoe paws and an all-black tail tip; the bobcat is a smaller-footed generalist with a tail black only on top.

documents.title: Lynx vs Caracal
documents.description: A lynx is a short-tailed, ruff-faced cat of cold forest with a usually spotted coat; a caracal is a plain tawny dry-country cat with far longer ear tufts and a much longer tail.

documents.title: Macaque vs Baboon
documents.description: Baboons are large, long-muzzled monkeys confined to Africa and Arabia; macaques are smaller, shorter-faced monkeys spread from North Africa across Asia, with tail length varying widely by species.

documents.title: Macaw vs African Grey Parrot
documents.description: The macaw group is a set of long-tailed, bright, loud American parrots, while the African grey is a single grey African species known instead for clear vocal imitation.

documents.title: Magpie vs Crow
documents.description: A magpie is a pied corvid with a very long graduated tail; a crow is uniformly black and compact with a short tail.

documents.title: Mole vs Shrew
documents.description: A mole has huge outward-turned digging forelimbs and eyes hidden beneath skin or fur; a shrew has small ordinary feet, visible eyes and a long twitching snout used above ground.

documents.title: Monarch vs Painted Lady
documents.description: The monarch is a milkweed specialist that is chemically defended and conservation-dependent; the painted lady is a host-plant generalist with a nearly global distribution.

documents.title: Moose vs Elk
documents.description: A moose is the largest deer, dark and solitary with palmate antlers; an elk in the North American sense is a smaller, tan, herd-living deer with tined antlers — and in Europe the word elk means the…

documents.title: Moose vs Red Deer
documents.description: The moose is a very large solitary browser of wet boreal forest with palmate antlers; the red deer is a smaller gregarious mixed feeder with branched tined antlers.

documents.title: Moth vs Hawk-Moth
documents.description: Hawk-moths are one family inside the moths, marked out by a torpedo body, narrow pointed forewings and powered hovering flight that most other moth families cannot manage.

documents.title: Mouse vs Guinea Pig
documents.description: A mouse is a tiny nocturnal omnivore from the murid line; a guinea pig is a much larger daytime caviomorph grazer that cannot synthesise vitamin C and needs the company of its own kind.

documents.title: Mule vs Alpaca
documents.description: A mule is a hybrid bred to carry weight; an alpaca is a camelid bred for fibre and is not used to carry loads at all.

documents.title: Mule vs Camel
documents.description: A mule is an equid shaped for insecure footing on broken ground; a camel is a camelid shaped for heat and water scarcity over open distance.

documents.title: Mule vs Cow
documents.description: A cow is a ruminant that extracts a great deal from poor forage slowly; a mule is a hindgut fermenter that extracts less but moves faster, which is why one ploughed heavy ground and the other carried…

documents.title: Mule vs Donkey
documents.description: A donkey is a self-reproducing species and the sire of every mule; the mule is the sterile offspring that keeps donkey extremities on a larger, horse-shaped body.

documents.title: Mule vs Elephant
documents.description: A mule is a domesticated hybrid bred to work; an elephant is a wild species whose working individuals are captive wild-type animals, not a domesticated form.

documents.title: Mule vs Guanaco
documents.description: A guanaco is a wild species that reproduces and is assessed on the Red List; a mule is a sterile hybrid manufactured from two domestic species and has no population to assess.

documents.title: Mule vs Horse
documents.description: A horse is a breeding species; a mule is a sterile first-cross hybrid that carries a horse's size and frame on a donkey's ears, feet and constitution.

documents.title: Mule vs Llama
documents.description: A mule is a hoofed odd-toed equid hybrid that digests in the hindgut, while a llama is a two-toed, pad-footed Andean camelid that ferments in a chambered forestomach.

documents.title: Mule vs Zebra
documents.description: Zebras are wild African equid species that reproduce in the wild, while a mule is a human-made cross between two domestic equids and carries no zebra ancestry.

documents.title: Newt vs Salamander
documents.description: Newts are a subgroup of salamanders that are more aquatic and rougher-skinned; salamander is the umbrella term for the whole tailed amphibian order.

documents.title: Nudibranch vs Sea Slug
documents.description: Nudibranchia is one defined order whose adults carry exposed gills and no shell, while sea slug is an informal umbrella that also covers shelled and internally shelled groups from other lineages.

documents.title: Octopus vs Cuttlefish
documents.description: An octopus is a boneless eight-armed manipulator that squeezes and explores; a cuttlefish is a ten-appendaged hoverer with a buoyancy-regulating cuttlebone.

documents.title: Octopus vs Nautilus
documents.description: A nautilus carries an external chambered shell and dozens of suckerless tentacles, while an octopus has no shell, eight suckered arms and colour-changing skin.

documents.title: Octopus vs Squid
documents.description: A squid has ten appendages — eight arms and two extensible feeding tentacles — plus an internal stiffening pen and mantle fins, while an octopus has eight arms and no skeletal support of any kind.

documents.title: Olm vs Axolotl
documents.description: The olm is a blind, unpigmented cave animal built for near-starvation and darkness; the axolotl is a pigmented, sighted lake salamander of shallow sunlit water.

documents.title: Osprey vs Albatross
documents.description: The osprey's wing is built for hovering and a powered plunge over coastal and inland water; the albatross's is built for near-effortless gliding across the open ocean.

documents.title: Osprey vs Bald Eagle
documents.description: An osprey is white underneath with a dark wrist patch and holds its wings kinked, while an adult bald eagle is dark underneath with a white head and tail and holds its wings flat.

documents.title: Osprey vs Eagle
documents.description: The osprey is the sole living species in Pandionidae with a fish-gripping foot, whereas eagle is a shape-and-size label covering many unrelated genera inside Accipitridae.

documents.title: Osprey vs Falcon
documents.description: The osprey is the only species in the family Pandionidae within Accipitriformes and takes live fish by dropping feet-first into water, while falcons form the family Falconidae in a separate order and…

documents.title: Osprey vs Frigatebird
documents.description: An osprey submerges to catch fish and is often robbed afterwards; a frigatebird never lands on water and takes much of its food from the surface or from other birds.

documents.title: Osprey vs Golden Eagle
documents.description: The golden eagle is a booted eagle with feathered legs that hunts mammals over uplands, while the osprey is a bare-legged fish specialist that cannot operate away from open water.

documents.title: Osprey vs Harpy Eagle
documents.description: The harpy eagle is a forest-interior hunter built to manoeuvre between trees and lift canopy mammals, while the osprey is an open-water specialist built to enter the surface and carry fish.

documents.title: Osprey vs Hawk
documents.description: The osprey is a single fish-specialised species in its own family that hunts by hovering over water, while hawk is a regional name for generalist accipitrids that hunt over land.

documents.title: Osprey vs Heron
documents.description: A heron hunts standing in shallow water and strikes with its bill; an osprey hunts from the air and takes fish with its feet.

documents.title: Osprey vs Kingfisher
documents.description: An osprey drops feet-first from height and grips fish in spiny toes; a kingfisher plunges bill-first from a low perch and grasps them in its beak.

documents.title: Osprey vs Kookaburra
documents.description: The kookaburra is a kingfisher that hunts dry land from a perch; the osprey is a raptor that gave up generalist hunting to specialise on live fish.

documents.title: Osprey vs Owl
documents.description: The osprey is a daytime visual hunter equipped to enter water, while owls are largely night hunters equipped to locate prey by sound and approach it without being heard.

documents.title: Osprey vs Pelican
documents.description: An osprey seizes one fish at a time in taloned feet; a pelican engulfs fish and water together in an expandable gular pouch and drains the water away.

documents.title: Osprey vs Penguin
documents.description: An osprey stays airborne and reaches into the water for a moment; a penguin gave up flight altogether so that it could pursue fish beneath the surface.

documents.title: Osprey vs Seagull
documents.description: The osprey is one fish-hunting raptor species that dives feet-first for live prey, while seagull is a loose name for many gull species that feed opportunistically at or near the surface.

documents.title: Osprey vs Secretary Bird
documents.description: The osprey is a compact plunge-diver that seizes fish in curved talons, while the secretary bird is a tall, long-legged terrestrial hunter that finds nearly all its food while walking.

documents.title: Osprey vs Shoebill
documents.description: The osprey is a globally distributed raptor that catches fish with its feet in flight; the shoebill is an African swamp specialist that catches them with an enormous hooked bill from a standing…

documents.title: Osprey vs Vulture
documents.description: The osprey is a live-fish specialist whose whole body is arranged around catching and carrying moving prey, while vultures are scavengers whose bodies are arranged around finding, walking on and…

documents.title: Osprey vs Wedge-tailed Eagle
documents.description: The wedge-tailed eagle is a true eagle of inland Australia taking mammals and carrion; the osprey is not an eagle at all but a coastal fish specialist in its own family.

documents.title: Ostrich vs Emu
documents.description: An ostrich has two toes, bare neck and thigh skin and is the tallest living bird; an emu has three toes and shaggy hair-like brown plumage.

documents.title: Ostrich vs Rhea
documents.description: Ostriches are the far larger African ratite with two toes and a bare neck; rheas are smaller South American birds with three toes and feathered upper necks.

documents.title: Otter vs Beaver
documents.description: An otter is a fish-eating carnivore with a round tapering tail; a beaver is a bark-eating rodent with a flat scaly paddle tail and dam-building habits.

documents.title: Owl vs Hawk
documents.description: Owls are nocturnal hunters built around hearing and silent flight; hawks are diurnal hunters built around vision, and the two are not closely related.

documents.title: Oyster vs Mussel
documents.description: An oyster cements one shell permanently to the substrate, while a mussel attaches with releasable byssal threads and retains limited mobility.

documents.title: Parrot vs African Grey Parrot
documents.description: Parrot names an entire order of several hundred species, while African grey names one African forest species inside it.

documents.title: Parrot vs Crow
documents.description: Parrots manipulate with a hooked bill and grasping feet and excel at vocal flexibility; crows manipulate with a straight bill and are notable for external tool use.

documents.title: Parrot vs Galah
documents.description: The galah is one species in the cockatoo family, and cockatoos are a family within the parrot order rather than a group standing apart from parrots.

documents.title: Parrot vs Macaw
documents.description: Macaw is a shape-and-size grouping of long-tailed, bare-faced New World parrots; parrot is the order that contains them along with every other parrot lineage.

documents.title: Peacock vs Chicken
documents.description: Peafowl are three wild pheasant species in which the male grows an annually moulted train, while the chicken is one domesticated species descended from red junglefowl and grows no train at all.

documents.title: Penguin vs Albatross
documents.description: Penguins turned their wings into dense diving flippers and hunt through the water column, while albatrosses turned theirs into locked soaring gliders and feed at the surface across enormous ranges.

documents.title: Pig vs Goat
documents.description: A pig is a single-stomached omnivore that works downwards into soil with its snout, while a goat is a four-stomached ruminant browser that works upwards into shrubs and low branches.

documents.title: Pig vs Wild Boar
documents.description: Domestic pigs are the domesticated form of the wild boar, bred for growth and fecundity, and feral populations revert toward boar-like traits within generations.

documents.title: Poison Dart Frog vs Mantella
documents.description: Poison dart frogs are an American family; mantellas are a Madagascan genus that arrived at the same bright, toxic, day-active design entirely separately.

documents.title: Polar Bear vs American Black Bear
documents.description: The polar bear is a sea-ice-dependent marine carnivore that hunts seals; the black bear is a forest omnivore that climbs and eats mostly plant material.

documents.title: Porcupine vs Echidna
documents.description: A porcupine is a placental rodent that gives birth to live young and gnaws plants; an echidna is an egg-laying monotreme with no teeth that probes soil for ants with a beak-like snout.

documents.title: Porpoise vs Orca
documents.description: Both are toothed whales, but the orca is the largest dolphin while porpoises belong to a separate family of very small cetaceans.

documents.title: Praying Mantis vs Mantis Shrimp
documents.description: The praying mantis is a terrestrial insect in Mantodea; the mantis shrimp is a marine stomatopod crustacean that is not a shrimp, and the shared name reflects only the folded raptorial forelimbs.

documents.title: Pronghorn vs Deer
documents.description: A pronghorn sheds a branched keratin sheath from a permanent bony core, while deer grow and cast whole bone antlers — two families, not two kinds of deer.

documents.title: Pufferfish vs Boxfish
documents.description: A pufferfish is a soft-bodied fish that inflates with water, while a boxfish is permanently rigid inside a fused bony carapace that cannot expand.

documents.title: Puffin vs Pelican
documents.description: A puffin's compact plated bill grips several small fish crosswise for carrying, while a pelican's huge bill and elastic pouch scoop water and fish together and strain the water away.

documents.title: Puffin vs Penguin
documents.description: Puffins are small northern auks that fly as well as swim, while penguins are larger southern seabirds whose wings became flippers and no longer generate flight.

documents.title: Python vs Boa
documents.description: Pythons lay eggs and are Old World; boas give birth to live young and are chiefly New World, and the two are separate families rather than variations on one.

documents.title: Rabbit vs Capybara
documents.description: A capybara is the largest rodent, semi-aquatic and living in large groups; a rabbit is a much smaller burrowing lagomorph from a different order.

documents.title: Rabbit vs Chinchilla
documents.description: A rabbit is a lagomorph built for grassland burrows and constant fibre; a chinchilla is a high-altitude rodent whose extreme coat density dictates cool, dry conditions and dust bathing instead of…

documents.title: Rabbit vs Hamster
documents.description: Rabbits are social, fibre-dependent lagomorphs; hamsters are solitary, food-hoarding rodents, and the two belong to different orders.

documents.title: Rabbit vs Hare
documents.description: Hares are born precocial — furred, sighted and mobile above ground — while rabbits are born altricial and helpless in a burrow, and almost every other difference follows from that.

documents.title: Rat vs Agouti
documents.description: An agouti is a long-legged Neotropical caviomorph with a vestigial tail and precocial young; a rat is a murid with a long scaly tail whose newborns are blind and hairless.

documents.title: Rat vs Bandicoot
documents.description: A true bandicoot is a marsupial that carries young in a rear-opening pouch; a rat is a placental rodent, and the Asian rodents called bandicoot rats are rats rather than bandicoots.

documents.title: Rat vs Beaver
documents.description: A rat is a small generalist rodent that slots into habitat already there; a beaver is a large semi-aquatic rodent that builds new habitat by damming running water.

documents.title: Rat vs Capybara
documents.description: A capybara is a tailless semi-aquatic grazer and the largest rodent alive; a rat is a small long-tailed omnivore from a genus that has spread worldwide with human traffic.

documents.title: Rat vs Cat
documents.description: A cat is a long-domesticated obligate carnivore adapted to hunting small mammals; a fancy rat is a recently domesticated omnivorous rodent of the kind that cats are adapted to hunt.

documents.title: Rat vs Chinchilla
documents.description: A chinchilla is a long-lived Andean specialist whose extreme coat dictates cool dry conditions and dust bathing; a rat is a short-lived climatic generalist that grooms itself and swims readily.

documents.title: Rat vs Cockroach
documents.description: A rat is an endothermic mammal that funds a constant body temperature with a large food intake; a cockroach is an ectothermic insect in an external skeleton whose whole pace of life is set by ambient…

documents.title: Rat vs Crow
documents.description: Both are wary, fast-learning urban omnivores, but a rat exploits the ground and the dark using scent, while a crow exploits the air and the daylight using sight.

documents.title: Rat vs Ferret
documents.description: A rat is an omnivorous rodent that lives in groups; a ferret is a domesticated carnivoran whose wild ancestor preyed on rodents of exactly that size.

documents.title: Rat vs Fox
documents.description: A fox is a wide-ranging canid predator that covers a large territory and breeds once a year; a rat is a small, sedentary, rapidly reproducing rodent that is one of the many things a fox eats.

documents.title: Rat vs Gerbil
documents.description: A gerbil is an arid-steppe murid with a furred tuft-tipped tail, long hind legs and water-sparing physiology; a rat is a damp-ground murid with a naked scaly tail that swims and climbs readily.

documents.title: Rat vs Guinea Pig
documents.description: A rat is a murid omnivore with helpless newborns and its own vitamin C supply; a guinea pig is a caviomorph herbivore whose young are born ready to walk and whose vitamin C must come from what it…

documents.title: Rat vs Hamster
documents.description: A rat is a colonial rodent kept in company, with a long naked tail and no pouches; a hamster is a solitary hoarder with a stub tail that carries seed in muscular cheek pouches.

documents.title: Rat vs Hedgehog
documents.description: A hedgehog is a spiny insectivore in Eulipotyphla with small pointed teeth and a curling defence; a rat is a rodent with gnawing incisors, plain fur and an escape-first response.

documents.title: Rat vs Mole
documents.description: A rat is a gnawing rodent with chisel incisors; a mole is an insectivorous eulipotyphlan with a full row of small sharp teeth and forelimbs rebuilt into digging spades.

documents.title: Rat vs Mole-Rat
documents.description: A rat is one genus of surface-living murid rodents, while mole-rat is a shared name for several separate lineages of burrowing rodents, some genuinely close to rats and some not.

documents.title: Rat vs Mongoose
documents.description: A mongoose is a cat-branch carnivoran with a fully furred tapering tail that forages by day; a rat is a murid rodent with a scaly tail that is mostly active after dark.

documents.title: Rat vs Mouse
documents.description: A mouse keeps a small head and oversized thin ears with a fine tail, while a rat has a heavier blunt-muzzled head, small-looking ears, a thick scaly tail and large hind feet at every age.

documents.title: Rat vs Owl
documents.description: An owl is a nocturnal predator built to locate and reach prey silently in darkness; a rat is a nocturnal prey animal built to stay out of the open and to distrust anything new.

documents.title: Rat vs Pigeon
documents.description: A rat exploits the horizontal, enclosed, night-time layer of a city from burrows and voids; a feral pigeon exploits the vertical, exposed, daylight layer from ledges, using flight to reach food.

documents.title: Rat vs Pine Marten
documents.description: A pine marten is a cat-sized mustelid with a cream throat bib and a thickly furred bushy tail; a rat is a much smaller rodent with no bib and a bare scaly tail.

documents.title: Rat vs Porcupine
documents.description: A rat is a small, quick-breeding, omnivorous murid with a fur coat; a porcupine is a large plant-eating rodent whose coat includes hardened quills and which invests heavily in very few young.

documents.title: Rat vs Rabbit
documents.description: A rabbit is a lagomorph with peg teeth and fibre-dependent hindgut fermentation living close to a decade; a rat is a rodent omnivore a fraction of its size with a two-to-three-year life.

documents.title: Rat vs Raccoon
documents.description: A raccoon is a mid-sized North American carnivoran that manipulates food with exceptionally sensitive forepaws; a rat is a small Old World rodent that opens food with ever-growing incisors and gets…

documents.title: Rat vs Shrew
documents.description: A shrew is an insect-eating eulipotyphlan with a long mobile snout and many small pointed teeth; a rat is a rodent with a blunt muzzle and two pairs of ever-growing gnawing incisors.

documents.title: Rat vs Snake
documents.description: A rat is a mammal in the genus Rattus; a snake is a legless reptile, and the rat snakes are simply snakes named for eating rodents rather than for any relationship to them.

documents.title: Rat vs Springhare
documents.description: A springhare is a bipedal hopping rodent with enormous hind legs and a long bushy tail; a rat is a quadrupedal runner with proportionate limbs and a sparsely haired scaly tail.

documents.title: Rat vs Squirrel
documents.description: A squirrel's tail is broad, bushy and plumed and it feeds in daylight; a rat's tail is thin and scaly and it moves mostly after dark.

documents.title: Rat vs Stoat
documents.description: A stoat has a short furred tail ending in a crisp black tip and a carnivoran's canines; a rat has a long scaly untipped tail and a rodent's ever-growing incisors.

documents.title: Rat vs Tenrec
documents.description: A rat is a murid rodent of the genus Rattus with ever-growing chisel incisors; a tenrec is an afrotherian mammal of Madagascar and Africa with a continuous row of small pointed teeth.

documents.title: Rat vs Weasel
documents.description: A rat is a rodent with ever-growing chisel incisors and a naked scaly tail; a weasel is a carnivoran with canines, a tubular body and a short furred tail.

documents.title: Rattlesnake vs Viper
documents.description: Rattlesnake names two American genera inside Viperidae; viper names the whole family, most of which has no rattle at all.

documents.title: Raven vs Crow
documents.description: A raven is a much larger corvid with a wedge-shaped tail, heavy bill and croaking call; a crow is smaller and neater with a fan-shaped tail and a flatter, higher caw.

documents.title: Ray vs Reef Manta Ray
documents.description: Most rays are bottom-living animals with the mouth underneath; the reef manta is one open-water species that filters plankton through a forward-facing mouth.

documents.title: Red Deer vs Roe Deer
documents.description: Red deer are large gregarious grazers with branched antlers and an autumn rut; roe deer are small solitary browsers with short antlers and a summer rut.

documents.title: Rhinoceros vs Hippopotamus
documents.description: Rhinos are odd-toed, horned and land-based, sitting with horses and tapirs; hippos are even-toed, hornless and water-bound, and their closest living relatives are the whales.

documents.title: Rook vs Crow
documents.description: An adult rook has bare pale skin at the base of a slim pointed bill plus shaggy thigh feathering, while a crow is fully feathered to the bill with a stouter arched bill and tidy flanks.

documents.title: Rook vs Magpie
documents.description: A rook is a uniformly black colonial corvid with a probing bill and a short tail, while a magpie is a pied, long-tailed territorial corvid that builds a domed nest.

documents.title: Rook vs Parrot
documents.description: The rook works on objects with a slim probing bill and no grasping foot, while parrots combine a hooked hinged bill with feet that hold items up to it, and only parrots learn to reproduce novel…

documents.title: Rook vs Pigeon
documents.description: A rook is a soil-probing corvid songbird that raises chicks on invertebrates; a pigeon is a seed-eating columbid that drinks by suction and raises squabs on crop milk.

documents.title: Rook vs Raven
documents.description: A raven is a much bulkier corvid with a heavy bill, shaggy throat hackles and a croaking voice, while a rook is mid-sized with a slim pointed bill, bare pale facial skin as an adult, and colonial…

documents.title: Rook vs Seagull
documents.description: A rook is a black corvid songbird that walks and probes soil with a long pale bill; a gull is a webbed-footed member of Laridae built to swim, soar and scavenge.

documents.title: Salmon vs Atlantic Salmon
documents.description: Atlantic salmon is one species in the genus Salmo that can survive spawning, while the Pacific salmon are a separate genus, Oncorhynchus, in which spawning is terminal.

documents.title: Salmon vs Trout
documents.description: Salmon are strongly migratory, and Pacific species die after spawning, while brown trout include both resident freshwater and sea-going forms of the same species.

documents.title: Saltwater Crocodile vs Nile Crocodile
documents.description: Paired ridges running forward from the eyes and reduced neck scales mark the saltwater crocodile, while a defined block of enlarged nuchal scutes behind the skull marks the Nile crocodile.

documents.title: Scorpion vs Spider
documents.description: Scorpions grasp with pincers and inject venom through a tail sting; spiders seize with fangs at the front of the body and produce silk.

documents.title: Sea Lion vs Seal
documents.description: Sea lions are eared seals that walk on rotated hind flippers and swim with long fore flippers; true seals have no ear flaps, cannot rotate the hind flippers, and propel themselves with the rear end.

documents.title: Sea Lion vs Walrus
documents.description: A sea lion is an eared seal with visible ear flaps that chases fish through open water; the walrus is the sole living odobenid, tusked in both sexes and feeding on shellfish taken from the seabed.

documents.title: Sea Turtle vs Tortoise
documents.description: A sea turtle is built for open ocean with flippers and a fixed streamlined shell; a tortoise is built for dry land with clawed columnar legs and a domed shell it can withdraw into.

documents.title: Seahorse vs Leafy Seadragon
documents.description: Seahorses grip with a prehensile tail and brood in a sealed pouch; the leafy seadragon cannot grip, broods on an exposed tail patch, and lives only off southern Australia.

documents.title: Seal vs Walrus
documents.description: True seals are earless pinnipeds that cannot rotate the hind flippers and hunt in mid-water; the walrus, also earless, walks on rotated hind flippers, grows tusks and feeds on the bottom.

documents.title: Shark vs Great White Shark
documents.description: Shark names several hundred species across about nine orders; the great white is a single lamnid species that is neither typical nor representative of them.

documents.title: Shark vs Ray
documents.description: Rays are flattened cartilaginous fish with gills on the underside and pectoral fins fused into a disc; sharks are typically cylindrical with side gills and swim with the tail.

documents.title: Snail vs Slug
documents.description: A slug is a gastropod that has lost or greatly reduced the external shell, trading protection and water retention for flexibility and freedom from a calcium requirement.

documents.title: Snake vs Legless Lizard
documents.description: A legless lizard blinks, has ear openings and can shed its tail; a snake does none of these, because limblessness evolved separately in the two lineages.

documents.title: Snow Leopard vs Leopard
documents.description: The snow leopard is a separate high-altitude Panthera species with pale smoky fur and a massively thick tail, not a cold-climate variant of the golden, tighter-rosetted leopard.

documents.title: Spider vs Tarantula
documents.description: A tarantula is a spider in the family Theraphosidae, distinguished by downward-striking parallel fangs, large size and exceptional longevity.

documents.title: Squid vs Cuttlefish
documents.description: A cuttlefish has a thick chambered cuttlebone controlling buoyancy and a fin running the whole mantle; a squid has a thin pen, fins at the rear, and a body built for open-water swimming.

documents.title: Squid vs Giant Squid
documents.description: Squid is a group name for hundreds of species, while giant squid refers specifically to Architeuthis, a bathypelagic animal with the largest known eyes and no light organs.

documents.title: Starfish vs Crown-of-Thorns Starfish
documents.description: Crown-of-thorns is one Indo-Pacific genus of spiny, many-armed coral specialists inside the class Asteroidea, which otherwise contains around 1,900 mostly five-armed species.

documents.title: Starfish vs Sea Urchin
documents.description: A starfish is an armed predator that often digests prey outside its body; a sea urchin is a spined grazing globe that scrapes algae with a specialised jaw apparatus.

documents.title: Swan vs Goose
documents.description: Swans are larger with very long necks for reaching submerged vegetation in deep water; geese are smaller and graze grass on land.

documents.title: Swan vs Pelican
documents.description: A swan grazes water plants with a flat waterfowl bill and flies with the neck out; a pelican scoops fish with a pouched bill and flies with the neck folded back.

documents.title: Tick vs Mite
documents.description: Every tick is a blood-feeding parasite of vertebrates and comparatively large, while the wider mites are mostly tiny and mostly free-living, with parasitism a minority lifestyle.

documents.title: Tortoise vs Box Turtle
documents.description: A box turtle's plastron is hinged so the shell shuts completely around it, while a tortoise's plastron is a single rigid plate that leaves the limb openings exposed.

documents.title: Toucan vs Hornbill
documents.description: Toucans are Neotropical piciforms with a plain hollow bill and an open nest hole; hornbills are Old World bucerotiforms that usually carry a casque and seal the nest cavity shut.

documents.title: Tuatara vs Iguana
documents.description: The tuatara is the last survivor of an order outside Squamata, while the iguana is an ordinary squamate lizard, despite the two looking broadly alike.

documents.title: Tuna vs Mackerel
documents.description: Tunas are deep-bodied Thunnini that keep swimming muscle warmer than the sea, whereas mackerels are slimmer scombrids that generally stay at ambient temperature.

documents.title: Turtle vs Tortoise
documents.description: A tortoise is a land-dwelling turtle in the family Testudinidae; turtle is the wider term for the whole order Testudines, most of which live in or near water.

documents.title: Viper vs European Viper
documents.description: Viper is the family Viperidae, spanning hundreds of species and four continents, while European viper is one species within it, Vipera berus, a pitless true viper of northern Eurasia.

documents.title: Vulture vs California Condor
documents.description: Vulture is a scavenging guild spread across two unrelated families, while the California condor is a single species, Gymnogyps californianus, inside the New World vulture family.

documents.title: Wasp vs Asian Giant Hornet
documents.description: Wasp is a common name spanning tens of thousands of species across many families, while the Asian giant hornet is a single species, Vespa mandarinia, inside the social-wasp genus Vespa.

documents.title: Weasel vs Stoat
documents.description: A stoat has a black-tipped tail in every season and coat; a least weasel has a shorter, wholly brown tail with no black tip.

documents.title: Whale vs Shark
documents.description: A whale is an air-breathing mammal descended from land animals; a shark is a fish that has always been marine, and the largest members of both groups converged independently on filter feeding.

documents.title: Wildebeest vs African Buffalo
documents.description: A wildebeest is a slope-backed antelope with smooth outward-curving horns, whereas an African buffalo is a bulkier bovine whose bulls grow a fused boss of horn across the forehead.

documents.title: Wolf vs Coyote
documents.description: A wolf is a large pack-hunting canid built for taking big prey; a coyote is a smaller, lighter, more generalist canid that thrives alone or in small groups, including in cities.

documents.title: Wolf vs Fox
documents.description: A wolf is a large pack hunter built around cooperative predation on big prey; a fox is a small solitary generalist that hunts alone and caches surplus food.

documents.title: Alligator vs Crocodile
documents.description: Snout profile, tooth arrangement and range — the three cues that actually separate them.

documents.title: Cheetah vs Leopard
documents.description: Solid spots against rosettes, and a sprinter's body against an ambush climber's.

documents.title: Falcon vs Eagle
documents.description: Two raptor groups in separate orders, with two completely different flight styles.

documents.title: Leopard vs Jaguar
documents.description: Rosette pattern, skull build and continent separate two spotted cats that are routinely mixed up.

documents.title: Lion vs Tiger
documents.description: Two big cats separated by continent and by social structure — pride life against solitary territory.

documents.title: Rabbit vs Guinea Pig
documents.description: Different mammalian orders, different social biology, different household demands.

documents.title: Wolf vs Dog
documents.description: What domestication actually changed between a wild canid and the domestic dog.

documents.title: Addax
documents.description: A desert antelope of the Sahara, now reduced to tiny remnant numbers in the wild, mainly in Niger and Chad.

documents.title: Adriatic Sturgeon
documents.description: Rivers draining to the Adriatic Sea, especially the Po basin in Italy.

documents.title: African Forest Elephant
documents.description: Rainforests of central and West Africa.

documents.title: African Penguin
documents.description: Breeds on the coasts and islands of South Africa and Namibia.

documents.title: African Wild Ass
documents.description: Arid deserts of the Horn of Africa, including parts of Eritrea and Ethiopia.

documents.title: African Wild Dog
documents.description: Fragmented populations across sub-Saharan Africa, with strongholds in southern and eastern Africa.

documents.title: Aldabra Giant Tortoise
documents.description: Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles, Indian Ocean, with introduced populations elsewhere.

documents.title: Amazon River Dolphin
documents.description: The Amazon and Orinoco river systems of South America.

documents.title: Amazonian Manatee
documents.description: The Amazon River basin of South America.

documents.title: American Burying Beetle
documents.description: Scattered sites in North America, much reduced from its former range.

documents.title: American Crocodile
documents.description: Coastal areas from southern Florida through Central America and the Caribbean to northern South America.

documents.title: American Eel
documents.description: Born in the Atlantic's Sargasso Sea; lives in fresh and coastal waters of eastern North America.

documents.title: Amur Leopard
documents.description: A leopard subspecies of the temperate forests of the Russian Far East and adjacent north-east China.

documents.title: Andean Bear
documents.description: Andean cloud forests and high grasslands of western South America.

documents.title: Andean Cat
documents.description: High Andes and Patagonian steppe of South America.

documents.title: Andean Condor
documents.description: The Andes and adjacent Pacific coasts of South America, from Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego.

documents.title: Angelshark
documents.description: Coastal waters of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean, much reduced.

documents.title: Aquatic Warbler
documents.description: Breeds in fen mires of central and eastern Europe and winters in West Africa.

documents.title: Archey's Frog
documents.description: A few forested areas of the North Island of New Zealand.

documents.title: Aruba Island Rattlesnake
documents.description: The island of Aruba in the Caribbean.

documents.title: Asian Elephant
documents.description: Scattered across South and Southeast Asia, from India and Sri Lanka to Thailand, Indonesia, and southern China.

documents.title: Asian Small-clawed Otter
documents.description: Wetlands, rivers, and coasts of South and Southeast Asia.

documents.title: Asiatic Black Bear
documents.description: Forests across much of Asia, from Iran and the Himalayas to Southeast Asia, China, and Japan.

documents.title: Asiatic Cheetah
documents.description: A few arid areas of Iran.

documents.title: Asiatic Lion
documents.description: The Gir Forest and surrounding areas of Gujarat, India.

documents.title: Atlantic Goliath Grouper
documents.description: Warm coastal waters of the western Atlantic.

documents.title: Atlantic Puffin
documents.description: Coasts and islands of the North Atlantic, breeding from North America to Europe.

documents.title: Axolotl
documents.description: Native only to the remnant lake and canal system of Xochimilco near Mexico City.

documents.title: Aye-aye
documents.description: Forests across Madagascar.

documents.title: Baiji
documents.description: Formerly the Yangtze River of China.

documents.title: Bali Myna
documents.description: The island of Bali, Indonesia.

documents.title: Banggai Cardinalfish
documents.description: A small area around the Banggai Islands of Indonesia.

documents.title: Banteng
documents.description: Forests of Southeast Asia, with populations on Java, Borneo, and the mainland.

documents.title: Barbary Macaque
documents.description: Mountain forests of Morocco and Algeria, with a famous introduced group on Gibraltar.

documents.title: Basking Shark
documents.description: Temperate coastal and open waters worldwide.

documents.title: Beluga Sturgeon
documents.description: The Caspian and Black Sea basins and their large rivers.

documents.title: Bengal Florican
documents.description: Grasslands of the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.

documents.title: Bigeye Tuna
documents.description: Tropical and subtropical open oceans worldwide.

documents.title: Black Abalone
documents.description: Rocky shores of California, USA, and Baja California, Mexico.

documents.title: Black-and-white Ruffed Lemur
documents.description: Rainforests of eastern Madagascar.

documents.title: Black-faced Spoonbill
documents.description: Coastal East Asia, breeding on islands off the Korean Peninsula and wintering farther south.

documents.title: Black-footed Cat
documents.description: Dry grasslands and scrub of southern Africa.

documents.title: Black-footed Ferret
documents.description: Grasslands of central North America, in reintroduced populations.

documents.title: Black Rhinoceros
documents.description: Found in fragmented populations across eastern and southern Africa, including Namibia, South Africa, Kenya, and Zimbabwe.

documents.title: Blue Crane
documents.description: Grasslands and farmland of southern Africa, mainly South Africa.

documents.title: Blue-throated Macaw
documents.description: A small area of seasonally flooded savanna in northern Bolivia.

documents.title: Blue Whale
documents.description: Found in oceans worldwide, migrating between cold feeding waters and warmer breeding areas.

documents.title: Bog Turtle
documents.description: Wetlands of the eastern United States.

documents.title: Bonobo
documents.description: Lowland rainforest south of the Congo River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

documents.title: Bornean Orangutan
documents.description: The island of Borneo, shared by Indonesia and Malaysia.

documents.title: Boulder Star Coral
documents.description: Caribbean and western Atlantic reefs.

documents.title: Bowmouth Guitarfish
documents.description: Coastal waters of the Indo-West Pacific.

documents.title: Bramble Cay Melomys
documents.description: Formerly Bramble Cay, a tiny island in the Torres Strait between Australia and New Guinea.

documents.title: Brown Spider Monkey
documents.description: Forests of northern Colombia and north-western Venezuela.

documents.title: Bumphead Parrotfish
documents.description: Coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific.

documents.title: Burmese Roofed Turtle
documents.description: Rivers of Myanmar.

documents.title: California Condor
documents.description: A small, intensively managed population in the south-western United States and Baja California, Mexico.

documents.title: California Tiger Salamander
documents.description: Grasslands and oak woodlands of California, USA.

documents.title: Cape Vulture
documents.description: Southern Africa.

documents.title: Carolina Parakeet
documents.description: Formerly the eastern and central United States.

documents.title: Central American River Turtle
documents.description: Rivers and lakes of southern Mexico and northern Central America.

documents.title: Chinese Alligator
documents.description: The lower Yangtze River region of eastern China.

documents.title: Chinese Bahaba
documents.description: Coastal waters of south-eastern China.

documents.title: Chinese Crocodile Lizard
documents.description: Streams and forests of southern China and northern Vietnam.

documents.title: Chinese Giant Salamander
documents.description: Mountain streams and rivers of central, southern, and eastern China.

documents.title: Chinese Paddlefish
documents.description: Formerly the Yangtze River of China.

documents.title: Chinese Pangolin
documents.description: Southern China, the Himalayan foothills, and parts of Southeast Asia.

documents.title: Chinese Sturgeon
documents.description: The Yangtze River and adjacent seas of China.

documents.title: Christmas Frigatebird
documents.description: Breeds only on Christmas Island in the Indian Ocean.

documents.title: Clouded Leopard
documents.description: Forests of South and Southeast Asia, from the Himalayan foothills to mainland Southeast Asia.

documents.title: West Indian Ocean Coelacanth
documents.description: Deep waters off eastern Africa, including around the Comoros.

documents.title: Common Hippopotamus
documents.description: Rivers, lakes, and wetlands across sub-Saharan Africa.

documents.title: Cotton-top Tamarin
documents.description: A small area of tropical forest in north-western Colombia.

documents.title: Crested Ibis
documents.description: East Asia; the wild population is centred in central China, with reintroductions elsewhere.

documents.title: Cross River Gorilla
documents.description: A small area of forested hills on the Nigeria-Cameroon border.

documents.title: Cuban Crocodile
documents.description: Two swamp areas of Cuba.

documents.title: Dama Gazelle
documents.description: The Sahara and Sahel of North Africa, now in tiny remnant populations.

documents.title: Darwin's Fox
documents.description: Forests of Chile, including Chiloe Island and a mainland population.

documents.title: Darwin's Frog
documents.description: Forest streams of southern Chile and Argentina.

documents.title: Dhole
documents.description: Scattered populations across South, Southeast, and East Asia.

documents.title: Dodo
documents.description: Formerly the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean.

documents.title: Drill
documents.description: Forests of Cameroon, Nigeria, and Bioko Island (Equatorial Guinea).

documents.title: Dugong
documents.description: Warm coastal waters of the Indian and western Pacific Oceans.

documents.title: Dusky Gopher Frog
documents.description: A tiny area of Mississippi in the southern United States.

documents.title: Dusky Shark
documents.description: Warm and temperate coastal and offshore waters worldwide.

documents.title: Dwarf Sawfish
documents.description: Coastal and estuarine waters of the Indo-West Pacific, much reduced.

documents.title: Eastern Gorilla
